paper_title: UniAVC: Unified Audio-Video Creation via Progressive Training and Asymmetric Scheduling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Unified audio-video creation requires single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit crossmodal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from single set of weights without task-specific adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniAVC achieves versatile audio-video generation and editing with competitive performance across different operating modes.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Audio-video content creation has advanced along several largely independent lines. Joint generators synthesize clip together with its soundtrack in single pass, achieving synchronization that cascaded pipelines struggle to match (Low et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Pham et al., 2026; HaCohen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025). Cross-modal models generate one modality conditioned on the other (Luo et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2025). Instruction-guided editors, extending paradigm established for images (Brooks et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023), modify an existing clip according to textual request (Chen et al., 2026c; Zheng et al., 2026), and control adapters attach conditioning to pretrained backbone, typically one adapter per control (Ben-Yosef et al., 2026). Each line has matured on its own terms, and each ships its own weights, training corpus, and task coverage. Operating across these decoupled paradigms carries severe cost for audio-video creation. Because existing tools specialize in either generation or editing, practical workflows must cascade independent models sequentially, for instance, by generating synchronized clip with joint model and then Project leader. Co-corresponding authors. 1 Preprint Figure 1: UniAVC performs joint audio-video generation, cross-modal generation in either direction, and instruction-guided editing of either or both modalities from one set of weights. modifying it with another instruction-guided editor. This sequential pipeline approach inherently degrades cross-modal coherence. When an editor modifies the visual stream without awareness of the soundtrack, it immediately breaks the precise synchrony established during initial generation. This drift accumulates through iterative edits, such as modifying ambient noise or restyling visual scene, forcing users to deploy dedicated resynchronization modules or explicit alignment losses just to repair the audio-visual match (Chen et al., 2026c; Liang et al., 2026). single model that natively unifies generation and editing across both modalities eliminates this vulnerability, establishing temporal correspondence once and retaining it across all downstream revisions (Huang et al., 2025). Realizing such unified framework, however, remains markedly harder than assembling specialized tools due to two compounding challenges. C1: Scarcity of paired audio-video supervision. High-quality datasets offering both precise audio-visual alignment for generation and instruction-guided editing pairs are far smaller than massive unimodal corpora. Training unified model directly on this limited paired data yields poor convergence, as the network must simultaneously master multiple competing objectives, including source preservation, text instruction compliance, and cross-modal synchronization (Zheng et al., 2026). Exacerbating this bottleneck, much of this scarce paired supervision is inefficiently spent teaching the model basic single-modality capabilities, such as rendering realistic visual motion or synthesizing clear acoustic signals. Because unimodal datasets already provide these isolated features in abundance, relying on paired data to learn them dilutes supervision signal through redundant learning, leaving inadequate learning capacity to capture the intricate cross-modal coupling that unimodal data alone can never supply. C2: Neglected information asymmetry between audio and video representations. Video latents maintain dense spatio-temporal structure across every frame (Blattmann et al., 2023; HaCohen et al., 2024), whereas audio codecs compress signals into far sparser sequence (Liu et al., 2023a; Evans et al., 2024). Consequently, clips visual token stream outnumbers its acoustic counterpart by more than an order of magnitude (HaCohen et al., 2026). Prevailing joint architectures nevertheless corrupt both modalities along single shared noise schedule, leaving this structural disparity unaddressed. Because video requires prolonged highnoise phase to establish global texture, identity, and motion before refining fine details, its optimal denoising trajectory differs fundamentally from that of audio, which settles into its final acoustic content much earlier  (Fig. 2)  . Aligning the shared schedule to video leaves audio artificially noisy long after it has Figure 2: Single vs. dual noise schedules. 2 Preprint converged, depriving the visual stream of clean cross-modal conditioning. Conversely, optimizing the schedule for audio forces video to commit to details prematurely before its global structure has formed. Ultimately, single rigid schedule fails both modalities. Beyond ignoring these distinct denoising trajectories, enforcing shared schedule severely restricts how the model explores noise states during training. Because each modality carries an independent noise level, the true state space during training is two-dimensional (Bao et al., 2023), rather than the single scalar timeline assumed in standard diffusion frameworks (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021). Locking both streams to equal noise levels forces training strictly along the diagonal of this 2D space, teaching the model only how to denoise symmetrically corrupted pairs. The core capabilities promised by unified framework, however, depend on off-diagonal, asymmetric noise states. Tasks such as restyling visual scene while preserving its soundtrack or generating video conditioned on existing audio require denoising corrupted video stream against completely clean audio. Because shared schedule never exposes the network to these off-diagonal configurations during training, the model encounters severe distribution shift at inference, asking it to execute conditioning behaviors it was never trained to perform. Our approach: UniAVC. To address these challenges, we introduce UniAVC, unified audio-video creation model built with progressive training and decoupled noise scheduling. We first establish full generative and editing competence in each modality using abundant unimodal corpora, then freeze both branches so that scarce paired data is used exclusively to train lightweight cross-modal bridges. This guarantees that paired supervision is dedicated entirely to cross-modal coupling rather than redundant single-modality learning. To address representation asymmetry and explore off-diagonal noise space, asymmetric modality-decoupled schedulers map shared timestep index onto two independently warped noise trajectories, curving the training region away from the symmetric diagonal. Complementing this, clean-branch subtasks explicitly supervise extreme boundary configurations that continuous warped curves cannot reach. This joint coverage unlocks intent-aware editing, which holds the preserved modality as clean reference to return the source material unchanged, as well as post-inference self-refinement, enabling the selective regeneration of an unsatisfactory branch conditioned on an accepted one. Our primary contributions are summarized as follows: Unified generation and editing framework. single model natively performs text-conditioned joint audio-video generation, bidirectional cross-modal synthesis, and instruction-guided editing of either or both modalities without requiring task-specific adapters  (Fig.1)  . Progressive training paradigm. By first mastering unimodal generative and editing capabilities on single-modality corpora before freezing both branches, our framework dedicates scarce paired datasets entirely to establishing cross-modal correspondence and temporal synchronization. Asymmetric noise-level scheduling. Modality-decoupled schedulers derive per-branch noise trajectories from shared timestep index to steer training off the diagonal of the 2D noise space, while clean-branch subtasks explicitly supervise extreme boundary states, together enabling intentaware editing and post-inference self-refinement. Extensive empirical evaluation. Comprehensive experiments across diverse generation and editing benchmarks demonstrate that UniAVC achieves performance competitive with specialized state-of-the-art baselines across all supported creation modes.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Joint Audio-Video Generation. Early joint synthesis coupled distinct modality-specific diffusion processes, either through shared cross-modal architectures (Ruan et al., 2023) or by aligning independently trained generators during inference (Xing et al., 2024). In parallel, cross-modal models synthesize one stream conditioned on the other, deriving alignment directly from the conditioning input rather than learning joint prior (Luo et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2025; Pham et al., 2025). Contemporary joint frameworks scale these paradigms by fusing twin backbones block by block (Low et al., 2025), integrating specialized experts into shared trunk (Wang et al., 2025a; OpenMOSS Team, 2026), estimating hierarchical spatio-temporal priors before generation (Liu et al., 2026a;b), or training end-to-end audio-visual foundation models (HaCohen et al., 2026). These advances leverage video diffusion transformers (Blattmann et al., 2023; HaCohen et al., 2024; Kong et al., 2024; Polyak et al., 2024) and audio latent diffusion models (Liu et al., 2023a; Evans et al., 3 Preprint 2024) that made high-resolution synthesis feasible. While these systems differ in their cross-modal interaction mechanisms, they universally share core design assumption: corrupting both modalities along single shared noise schedule, key limitation our work directly re-examines. Joint Audio-Video Editing. Instruction-guided audio-video editing requires modifying specific target attributes while preserving unmentioned content intact. To address the resulting data scarcity, JAVEdit (Chen et al., 2026c) employs an agent-in-the-loop curation pipeline and benchmark, whereas SpongeBob (Liang et al., 2026) reformulates editing as self-supervised inpainting on unannotated clips. InstructAV2AV (Zheng et al., 2026) trains an end-to-end joint editor using gated attention to balance instruction compliance against source preservation. For efficiency, AVControl (Ben-Yosef et al., 2026) deploys lightweight per-modality control adapters, whereas JoVA (Huang et al., 2025) and the concurrent MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026) unify generation and editing within shared representation space. These existing methods rely heavily on scarce paired editing data to establish basic single-modality competence. In contrast, UniAVC derives single-modality capabilities from abundant unimodal corpora, dedicating its paired supervision exclusively to cross-modal coupling. Non-uniform Noise Schedules. Diffusion models typically apply single noise level across an entire sample, but two distinct lines of work depart from this assumption. The first varies noise levels across positions within single modality, using independent per-frame noise (Chen et al., 2024), sliding temporal windows (Ruhe et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024b), or monotonic token schedules (Wu et al., 2023a). The second varies noise across modalities: UniDiffuser (Bao et al., 2023) samples independent noise for image and text, while MoNL (Kim et al., 2024a) varies noise along temporal and modal axes to enable arbitrary conditional generation. Extending this to audio and video, MoVA (OpenMOSS Team, 2026) draws timesteps independently per stream. While this covers more of the joint noise space, uncoupled sampling breaks the deterministic link between noise pairs and the step counter, leaving the model without structured conditioning during inference. Orthogonally, rectifiedflow models scale global schedules by sequence length (Esser et al., 2024), acknowledging density disparities while still enforcing single trajectory per sample. In contrast, UniAVC assigns dedicated schedules per modality anchored to shared step counter. Trajectories remain phase-locked as their magnitudes diverge, keeping the denser visual stream at high noise long after the acoustic stream converges. Finally, two clean-branch subtasks explicitly supervise boundary states where one stream remains clean, directly enabling single-modality editing and post-inference branch refinement.

The expectation is taken over the data distribution of the tuple, the independent noise draws, and the noise-level pair. θ θ 3.2 UNIFIED GENERATION AND EDITING Backbone. We build upon LTX-2.3 (HaCohen et al., 2026), where video and audio tokens are processed by separate transformer stacks, each equipped with dedicated self-attention, feed-forward blocks, and adaptive normalization (Peebles & Xie, 2023), while both attend to shared text embedding. The two branches intersect exclusively at per-block bridges, consisting of an audio-tovideo cross-attention layer where video queries attend to audio keys and values, and symmetric video-to-audio layer with swapped roles. Each bridge operates as gated residual module whose scale, shift, and gate are derived via adaptive normalization from noise level. The critical design choice lies in which noise level modulates each path. Crucially, each bridge is modulated by the noise level of the opposing branch, such that the gate regulating information flow from audio into video is function of σa, while its mirror in the visual branch depends on σv (Fig. 3a). In-Context Reference Conditioning. Rather than adding dedicated input branches, we adopt in-context conditioning for diffusion transformers (Huang et al., 2024) by concatenating reference latents, patchified by the same encoder, onto the target sequence of their corresponding modality. temporal offset applied to the reference rotary embeddings and learned token-type embedding separate the two sequence spans. Prior in-context video editing works assign reference tokens the exact positions of their target counterparts, enforcing strict spatiotemporal alignment between input and output (Chen et al., 2026a; Polaczek et al., 2025). However, this strict alignment fails when editing instructions require relocating or transforming content. Furthermore, naive concatenation allows reference tokens to attend to noisy target tokens, causing the conditioning signal to drift and degrade as noise increases. We prevent this by applying attention masks that allow target queries to attend to the full sequence while restricting reference queries to read only the uncorrupted reference span. The same isolation extends to cross-modal bridges, where reference queries in one branch can attend to the partner modalitys reference span but not its noisy target (Fig. 3a). 3.3 PROGRESSIVE TRAINING PARADIGM Two Stages. Paired audio-video editing datasets are scarce compared to the abundant unimodal corpora used to pretrain single-modality generators. Training joint editor directly on limited paired data forces the model to learn source preservation, instruction following, and cross-modal synchronization simultaneously, multi-task burden known to cause poor convergence (Zheng et al., Preprint 2026). To resolve this bottleneck, we decompose training into two stages: Unimodal Pretraining and Alignment Finetuning (Fig. 3b). The first stage establishes full generative and editing competence within each independent branch using modality-specific data. The second stage integrates both pretrained branches into the dual-branch backbone and updates only the cross-modal bridges alongside their adaptive normalization parameters. This strategy dedicates scarce paired datasets entirely to learning cross-modal alignment and temporal synchronization, which cannot be acquired from unimodal corpora alone. Conditioning Dropout. Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022) is enabled by randomly dropping the text prompt and reference latents independently during training. This exposes two distinct guidance axes at inference rather than single scale: the text axis governs instruction compliance, while the reference axis enforces source fidelity, allowing the two signals to be traded off explicitly during sampling. Furthermore, we include reconstruction subtask where the reference is designated as the target latent under null-edit instruction. This subtask provides explicit supervision for source preservation, directly counteracting the tendency of instruction-tuned models to alter regions unmentioned by the prompt. 3.4 ASYMMETRIC MODALITY-DECOUPLED SCHEDULERS Noise-Level Pair. Standard diffusion models typically sample single noise level per trajectory across all modalities (Bao et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024a), imposing the constraint σv = σa on Eq. 1. In contrast, with independently drawn noise vectors ϵv and ϵa, Eq. 1 defines family of corrupted distributions parameterized by the noise-level pair (σa, σv): qσa,σv (v, v0, a0) = (cid:0)v; (1 σv)v0, σ vI(cid:1)N (cid:0)a; (1 σa)a0, σ2 aI(cid:1), σa, σv [0, 1], (3) from which each branch regresses its target velocity. Because each branch conditions on the partner stream at its respective noise level, three distinct operational regimes emerge. On the diagonal (σa = σv), the model observes partner stream that is informative yet noisy, regressing velocity that averages over the partners uncertainty. When σa = 0, the partner stream is completely clean, allowing the video branch to treat audio as an uncorrupted constraint, which is essential for cross-modal generation and audio-preserving editing. Standard shared schedules visit only the diagonal  (Fig. 2)  , preventing the model from encountering the clean-partner boundary regimes needed for downstream editing and cross-modal generation tasks. Audio thus resolves ahead of video, allowing cross-modal bridges to pass progressively cleaner acoustic representation into the video branch, establishing natural temporal ordering from two warped schedules on single index rather than manual staging. < σ(i) Clean-Branch Subtasks. Because continuous schedules rarely reach the boundary faces where σ = 0 for an individual branch, we explicitly supervise these boundary conditions to support crossmodal generation and single-modality editing. Specifically, we assign small fraction of training samples to subtasks where one stream is pinned to its uncorrupted latent and its loss is masked, such as audio-conditioned video generation (σa = 0, Ma = 0 in Eq. 2) or its visual counterpart. Masking the loss reflects that the uncorrupted stream serves as fixed conditioning signal rather than regression target, which guarantees that single-modality edits leave the non-target stream untouched Preprint (Sec. 3.5). Concurrent work (Liang et al., 2026) adopts similar modes by switching between fixed discrete configurations; in contrast, our unified step index dynamically positions each denoising step along distinct off-diagonal pairs within continuous noise-level space. 3.5 SELECTIVE REGENERATION Dual-schedule training expands the domain of observed noise-level pairs, directly enabling two specialized inference modes. By holding one branch at σ = 0 while denoising the other, these modes remain in-distribution, as clean-branch subtasks explicitly supervise these boundary regimes. Intent-Aware Editing. Users frequently require targeted edits that modify one modality while preserving the other, such as restyling video while retaining original dialogue. Single-modality editors treat the preserved stream as static context uncoupled from the output, causing the edited result to drift out of alignment (Huang et al., 2025; Ben-Yosef et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026). In contrast, we pin the preserved branch at σa = 0 as reference latent. The visual branch thus conditions directly on clean latents a0 rather than corrupted trajectory aσa , referencing acoustic timing, onsets, and lip motion at every step. Because no denoising steps are applied to the pinned branch, the sampler returns the exact source latent rather than an approximated resynthesis, guaranteeing exact preservation by construction. Both editing directions operate without task-specific adapters, whereas evaluating this setup on single-schedule baseline constitutes an out-of-distribution extrapolation. Self-Refinement. When joint generation yields only one satisfactory modality, users can retain the accepted stream and regenerate the other rather than resampling the entire pair. For instance, to refine generated audio latent ˆa0 while keeping the video branch fixed, second denoising trajectory is executed after the initial pass completes. Unlike two-stage inference guidance (Liang et al., 2026), which adjusts conditioning within single trajectory, self-refinement re-noises ˆa0 to noise level σa = λ and denoises along rescaled schedule λσ(i) while holding the visual branch clean at σv = 0. This mechanism mirrors the pinning and in-context conditioning of intent-aware editing, differing only in the source of the pinned stream, which uses the first-pass generated latent rather than user-supplied input.

sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Implementation Details. We initialize each branch from the pretrained weights of LTX-2.3 (HaCohen et al., 2026) and train it in the two stages of Sec. 3.3. Each stage runs at 720p over 121 frames at 24 fps with 16 kHz mono audio, with AdamW optimizer at learning rate of 1 105 and weight decay 0.01 in bf16. Table 1 gives the sample budget of each training stage, where alignment finetuning spends under 1% of the unimodal pretraining in total. Schedulers run with kv = 9 and ka = 2. The text and reference dropout probabilities are both set to 0.1. For joint generation, we compare against Ovi (Low et al., 2025), JavisDiT (Chen et al., 2026c), UniVerse-1 (Wang et al., 2025a), JoVA (Huang et al., 2025), LTX-2.3 (HaCohen et al., 2026), and MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026). Finally, we compare against some representative specialists including MMAudio (Cheng et al., 2025) and VinTAGe (Kushwaha & Tian, 2025) for video-to-audio; and AVTok (Pham et al., 2026) and TempoTokens (Yariv et al., 2024) for audio-to-video generation. 4.2 MAIN RESULTS Across both evaluations, UniAVC performs competitively against selected baselines across all supported tasks. Specifically, UniAVC outperforms prevailing methods on most joint audio-video editing metrics (Tab. 2) and simultaneously achieves robust results in both joint and cross-modal generation settings (Tab. 3). Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 4 further demonstrate that UniAVC maintains precise instruction following, high perceptual fidelity, and robust preservation of character identity and unedited regions, across various tasks, addressing key limitations often observed in the representative InstructAV2AV and MiniMax-H3. 4.3 ABLATION STUDY To evaluate the impact of the progressive training recipe, the two inference modes and the asymmetric dual schedulers proposed in Sec. 3, we conduct an ablation study on JAVEditBench, of which the results are shown in Tab. 4. Training Paradigm. Progressive training outperforms single-stage finetuning across all metrics, primarily on cross-modal ones (AVQ, AQ) rather than visual quality alone, confirming that reserving paired data for the second stage effectively dedicates capacity to cross-modal alignment. 8 Preprint Figure 4: Qualitative comparisons for joint editing on JAVEditBench. Intent-aware editing improves audio quality by conditioning on uncorrupted source latents, whereas self-refinement yields the largest gains in instruction compliance by re-noising single branch against an accepted counterpart. The two modes operate complementarily, with their combination achieving peak cross-modal synchronization (AVS, AVQ) and overall performance. Scheduler Shift. Removing schedule asymmetry causes notable drops in cross-modal metrics (AQ, AVQ) with minimal impact on visual quality, demonstrating the limitation of imposing equal noise levels on intrinsically distinctive streams. Besides, excessively increasing shift strengths degrades performance across most metrics, showing that schedule warping saturates beyond moderate shift.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present UniAVC, unified framework for audio-video generation and editing, capable of textconditioned joint generation, bidirectional cross-modal synthesis, and instruction-guided editing of either or both streams without requiring task-specific adapters or secondary checkpoints. This capability rests on two key designs: progressive training establishes unimodal competence from singlemodality corpora to reserve paired data for cross-modal bridges, while asymmetric schedulers drive independently warped noise trajectories to access the off-diagonal configurations required for editing and cross-modal generation, complemented by clean-branch subtasks that supervise boundary states. Together, these mechanisms enable intent-aware editing to return preserved modalities unchanged 9 Preprint and self-refinement to selectively regenerate flawed modalities. These operational modes differ solely in conditioning and supervision rather than architecture, though coverage remains confined to 1D trajectory and two boundary faces rather than the full noise-pair space, and cross-modal bridges align representations without repairing unimodal deficits. AI Use Statement. Generative AI tools were employed exclusively to polish the manuscript and enhance text clarity and readability. This assistance was strictly limited to linguistic refinement; generative AI played no role in research ideation, data collection or generation, mathematical proofs, experimental design or implementation, data analysis, or the formulation of scientific claims. All AI-assisted revisions were thoroughly reviewed and verified by the authors to guarantee accuracy. The authors retain full responsibility for the entire final manuscript, including all methods, data, analyses, and conclusions.

Unimodal Pretraining optimizes the video and audio branches independently on modality-specific corpora without paired audio-video samples. Alignment Finetuning consumes paired data to establish cross-modal alignment, which unimodal pretraining cannot provide. Unimodal Pretraining (V). We draw 34.3M samples from 15.3M pool constructed from BooguImage (Chen et al., 2026b), Ditto (Bai et al., 2025), and OpenVE-3M (He et al., 2025). Following Wu et al. (2026), still-image tasks are retained in the mixture to improve frame fidelity and edit diversity. Because image samples consume fewer tokens than 10s video clips, we assign sampling probabilities of 0.33 to each image task and 0.17 to each video task, maintaining an effective balance between spatial fidelity and temporal training dynamics respectively. Unimodal Pretraining (A). We draw 54.9M samples from 14.9M pool built from AudioSet (Gemmeke et al., 2017), VGGSound (Chen et al., 2020), WavCaps (Mei et al., 2024), Emilia (He et al., 2024), LibriTTS (Zen et al., 2019), AudioEdit (Tian et al., 2026), and the ISCSLP 2026 CoT-TTS Challenge (Xue et al., 2026), sampling the two audio tasks with equal probability of 0.50. Because speech samples outnumber environmental sound samples by roughly 5:1 within single task identifier, we reweight the sampler toward domain-level parity rather than task-level parity. Alignment Finetuning. We draw 0.67M paired samples from 0.74M pool comprising TAVGBench (Mao et al., 2024), JAVEdit (Chen et al., 2026c), and the held-out split of InsAVE-80K (Zheng et al., 2026), assigning sampling probabilities of 0.30 to joint generation and 0.70 to joint editing. This stage operates in sub-epoch regime, with 0.67M draws completing roughly 0.90 of single pass over the 0.74M pool. Tab. A1 details the per-task breakdown of these dataset sizes and sampling counts. A1.2 SUBTASK MIXTURES In both training stages, each batch samples task according to the probabilities in Tab. A1. Alignment Finetuning further mixes multiple objectives within each task, allowing single paired sample to supervise off-diagonal noise configurations in the (σa, σv) space. Specifically, the joint generation task assigns weights of 0.7 to the standard objective, 0.1 to reconstruction, and 0.1 to each cleanbranch subtask. The joint editing task assigns weights of 0.8 to the standard objective and 0.1 to each self-refinement subtask. 16 Preprint The reconstruction objective uses the reference as the target alongside an instruction requesting no modification. This supplies the sole supervisory signal for leaving content unaltered, counteracting instruction-following losses that reward target changes without penalizing collateral edits. Cleanbranch subtasks explicitly supervise the boundary regime where σ = 0, which is essential for crossmodal generation and single-modality editing, and differ based on whether reference conditioning is present. A1.3 EVALUATION METRICS Each benchmark scores different metric set, and the same abbreviation denotes different quantities across benchmarks. The metrics are listed below under the benchmark they come from. JAVEditBench. Six metrics span five dimensions, combining learned perceptual models with multimodal judge. Visual quality (VQ) is scored by VTSS, the aesthetic model adopted by Koala-36M (Wang et al., 2025b). Audio quality (AQ) is scored by UTMOSv2 (Baba et al., 2024). Audio-visual synchrony (AVS) is scored by SyncNet as implemented in LatentSync (Li et al., 2025). Instruction compliance (IC), video fidelity (VF) and AV quality (AVQ) are judged by Qwen3-Omni (Xu et al., 2025): whether the edit executes the instruction, whether unrelated content is preserved, and the overall joint quality of the edited clip. InsAVE-80K. Six metrics span video, audio and audio-visual properties. Frechet Video Distance (FVD) measures visual realism and spatiotemporal coherence using VideoMAE (Tong et al., 2022) backbone. Frechet Audio Distance (FAD) is the analogous measure for audio, over VGGish (Diwakar & Gupta, 2024) embeddings. Text-video alignment (TV-A) and text-audio alignment (TA-A) measure agreement between the instruction and each generated modality, using VideoCLIP-XL (Wang et al., 2024) and CLAP (Wu et al., 2023b). Audio-video alignment (AV-A) measures semantic coherence between the two generated streams using ImageBind (Girdhar et al., 2023). PEAVS predicts mean opinion score for audio-visual synchrony (Goncalves et al., 2024). VGGSound. Four metrics are reported under the protocol of Pham et al. (2026). FVD (Unterthiner et al., 2019) and FAD (Kilgour et al., 2019) measure video and audio quality, DeSync (Iashin et al., 2024) measures temporal synchronization, and the ImageBind score (IB) (Girdhar et al., 2023) measures semantic alignment. Because the Frechet distances are computed against ground truth, FVD requires generated video and is reported only for audio-to-video, while FAD requires generated audio and is reported only for video-to-audio; DeSync and IB are evaluated for both directions. The empty cells in Tab. 3 reflect this, rather than missing measurements. Verse-Bench. Six metrics are reported following Huang et al. (2025). Motion score (MS) is computed from RAFT (Teed & Deng, 2020) optical flow. Aesthetic score (AS) averages MANIQA (Yang et al., 2022), aesthetic-predictor-v2-5 and Musiq (Ke et al., 2021). Production quality (PQ) comes from AudioBox-Aesthetics (Tjandra et al., 2025). Text-audio consistency (CS) is LAION-CLAP (Wu et al., 2023b) score. Lip-sync confidence (LSE-C) is produced by SyncNet (Chung & Zisserman, 2016). Word error rate (WER) is computed by transcribing generated audio with Whisper-large-v3 (Radford et al., 2023). LSE-C is scored only on human-speech samples, since the metric requires visible mouth motion. A2.3 ABLATIONS Tab. 4 isolates individual design factors relative to the default configuration, while Fig. A3 illustrates the performance of both inference modes on matched inputs. We observe that intent-aware editing and self-refinement modes both allow for high-quality editing or enhancing target modality, while losslessly preserving non-target counterpart and maintaining their alignment. A2.4 LIMITATIONS UniAVC incurs notable computational overhead during both training and inference. The twostage recipe requires substantial resources, consuming large-scale unimodal data during pretraining before alignment finetuning begins. Inference latency also precludes real-time deployment because every request requires full denoising trajectories across both streams, with self-refinement adding second pass over the target modality. Furthermore, performance is constrained by the complexity of instruction prompts in the training set. Because paired corpora contain few compositional requests specifying multiple concurrent edits, the model may execute multi-goal instructions imperfectly.
